title: Previewing a draft before it is public
metaTitle: Preview the draft in the real template
excerpt: Writers should see the real page template before a draft is public. A preview that looks different from the site becomes a second design they will polish by mistake.
alt: Curved library shelves packed with books, seen from a balcony. The shelves of drafts fit a piece about previewing a page before it is public.
caption: Read it in the template, while it is still a draft. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a CMS draft preview show?
faqs.answer: The same template as the public page: type, color, line length, images at the real crop, and the navigation the headline has to live with. The admin form is for editing fields. It is not a preview. If the preview uses a fallback font or sample content the public page will not have, writers will polish the wrong design.

faqs.question: How do you share a draft without publishing it?
faqs.answer: Use a link that shows the draft in the template, marked as a draft, with noindex so a leaked URL is less likely to be treated as public. Keep it out of the nav and the sitemap. Let people comment beside the page, and keep publish as a separate action from viewing.

faqs.question: What should a writer check in preview?
faqs.answer: Whether the headline wraps, whether the first paragraphs say what the page is for, and whether images crop the subject. Read it at a phone width. An empty image should look empty, so the hole is fixed in the draft rather than hidden by sample content that only exists in preview.

markdown:
A cms draft preview shows the real template before the page is public. The person writing should see the type, the measure, the images, and the form as the visitor will see them. A preview that looks different from the site creates a second design, and the writer will polish the wrong one.

The admin screen is for fields. The preview is for the page. They are not substitutes.

## The same template, with a draft flag

Render the draft through the components the public page uses. The headline component, the body, the figures, the closing band. If the public site is server rendered, the preview should be that render, pointed at unpublished content. A CSS skin that "looks like" the site, maintained inside the CMS, will drift the first time the site changes a spacing token.

Hanabi's public stories are edited in Payload and rendered by the site. The useful preview is that render. The admin form can show the title and the body as fields. It cannot show whether the headline wraps badly, whether an image crops the subject, or whether the excerpt looks like a tease instead of a summary. Those show up in the template.

Pass a flag that says this is a draft. The flag does two jobs. It lets the query load unpublished content, and it lets the page mark itself so nobody confuses a preview for the live site. A quiet banner, "Draft, not public," is enough. Do not let the banner shove the layout down so far that the preview no longer matches production. Reserve its space, or overlay it, and check both themes if you have them.

Unpublished means unpublished. The preview URL should not be linked from the nav, the sitemap, or the RSS feed. It should send a noindex header or meta tag so a leaked link is less likely to be treated as a public page. Share it with the people who are writing, not with the world. A preview that is secretly public is just a second live site with worse QA.

## What the writer is checking

They are checking the sentences in context. A headline that fit the field may break the hero. A paragraph that looked fine in a narrow admin column may be a wall of text in the template, or a lonely line. The preview is where line length is visible. If the template has a measure, the writer sees it. If the preview uses a different measure, they will edit toward the wrong width, and you will have trained them to write for a page that does not exist.

They are checking images at the real crop. The slot on the page has a ratio. The photograph should be judged in that ratio, with the alt text beside the decision, not only in a media library tile. A portrait jammed into a landscape slot is obvious in the template and invisible in a square thumbnail.

They are checking the order of the page. Heading, support, action, proof, close. A CMS that lists fields in database order may not match the page order. The preview is the order that matters. If a field does not appear, the writer should see that absence on the page, not discover it after publish.

Google's guidance on [people-first content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks whether the title describes the page and whether someone leaves able to do the thing they came for. Preview is where you ask those questions before the URL is public. Read the headline as a stranger. Read the first two paragraphs. If they do not say what the page is for, fix them in the draft. Do not publish in order to find out.

## What a false preview costs

Writers believe the preview. If it uses a fallback font, they will add line breaks that only make sense in that font. If it omits the navigation, they will not notice a headline that collides with it. If it shows a desktop frame only, the phone layout will be a surprise on launch morning.

Match the type, the colors, and the breakpoints. Give the writer a way to view a narrow width without asking them to become a front-end developer. A single toggle or the browser's own device mode, against the real page, is enough. A screenshot you email is already stale, and it cannot be clicked. Links in a draft should go where they will go in public, or they should be obviously dead in the preview, so a bad href is caught.

Blocks that only exist in the CMS preview, such as a sample testimonial that is hard-coded there, will be written around. Then the public page, without the sample, falls apart. Preview data should be the draft's data. Empty states in preview should look like empty states in production, so the writer sees that a missing image leaves a hole. Fill the hole in the draft or change the template. Do not paper over it in the preview only.

Time and identity need the same honesty. If a byline or a date will be public, show them. If a draft has no date yet, show that it has no date, rather than inventing "today" in preview and "the publish date" later. The writer is checking a document, not a mock.

## Sharing it without publishing

The founder needs to open the preview without an account in the CMS, or with a role that cannot press publish by mistake. A signed link that expires is a good fit. A link that never expires and is not noindexed will leak, and leaked drafts get quoted. Expire the link. Keep the draft status intact when the link dies.

Comments belong outside the pixels. A note in the margin of the preview, or a short list beside it, is better than asking someone to edit the live-looking headline to leave feedback. The preview should stay a faithful render. Feedback can live next to it. If they need to try a sentence, they do it in the draft fields and refresh the preview. That round trip is the point. What they approve is what the template will ship.

Permissions should make "publish" a separate act from "see the draft." The person checking copy is not always the person who should put it on the public site. A preview that is also the publish button will be pressed because the page looks done. Separate the controls. Looking done in the template is the cue for a review, not the cue for the DNS-level truth of a public URL.

When the draft is approved, publishing should not change the layout. If it does, the preview was not the template. Treat a post-publish visual change as a bug. The fix is to make preview and public share code, not to maintain a checklist of differences.


## Metadata is part of the page you are previewing

The title tag, the excerpt, and the social title are easy to ignore because they sit beside the template rather than inside the hero. Preview them anyway. A draft page that looks right and carries an old title, or an excerpt that teases instead of summarizing, will publish that mistake with one click. Show the title and the excerpt next to the render, in the same review, so the writer accepts them together.

Alt text belongs in that review when the image is informative. The preview can show the alt beside the figure, or in an obvious field that the writer sees while looking at the crop. An alt that describes a different photograph from the one in the slot is a bug you can catch only when both are visible. Decorative images should be marked as decorative in the same pass, so the public page does not announce a filename.

Links get a hover or a visible href in preview if you can offer it without cluttering the article. A button that says "read the guide" and points at the homepage is the sort of error a visual mock will not show. Click through on the draft, inside the preview, before you call the copy done. Internal links that assume a published slug should resolve to the draft when the target is also a draft, or they should say the target is not public yet. A preview that 404s its own related links trains the writer to ignore broken paths.

Do this with the real production styles loaded. A preview environment that is "close enough" on fonts will be wrong on line breaks, and line breaks are what the writer is judging. If the preview host cannot load the real assets, it is not a preview. It is a staging approximation, and approximations are how the second design sneaks back in.


## A check before you trust it

Write a throwaway draft and open the preview next to a published page.

- The type, colors, and width match.
- Unpublished content is visible here and absent from the public nav and sitemap.
- The preview document is marked noindex, and the page says it is a draft.
- Images crop as they will crop in public.
- An empty required field looks empty, not filled with sample content.
- Publishing does not change the layout you approved.

Then open the preview on a phone. The second design often hides there, in a padding value the desktop preview never touched.

Redirects are the next publishing hazard, once real URLs start to change. [Redirects after you change the URLs](/blog/redirects-after-you-change-the-urls) covers mapping every old address to the closest new page. A careful preview does not help the person who still has last year's link. They need the map.

When you want drafts reviewed in the real template before anything is public, see [Hanabi's services](https://tryhanabi.com/#services). The preview is the site, shown early.
